'''''Pentaglottis''''' is a [[monotypic]] genus of flowering plants in the family [[Boraginaceae]]. It is represented by a single species, '''''Pentaglottis sempervirens''''', commonly known as '''green alkanet'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> or '''evergreen bugloss''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=PESE10|taxon=''Pentaglottis sempervirens''|access-date=31 January 2016}}</ref> and it is one of [[Alkanet|several related plants]] known as '''alkanet'''.  It is a bristly, [[perennial plant]] native to southwestern Europe, in northwest [[Iberian Peninsula|Iberia]] and France. 

==Description==
''Pentaglottis sempervirens'' is a [[Perennial plant|perennial]], that has a deep [[Taproot|tap root]]. 
It grows up to approximately {{cvt|60|-|90|cm|1}} tall with a roughly hairy stem. It has broadly ovate,<ref name="RHS"/> or pointed oval leaves and the lower leaves have leaf stalks. Both the leaves and stem can cause skin irritation.<ref name="RHS"/> It can retain its green leaves through the winter.

Green alkanet blooms in spring and summer, while the ground is moist.<ref name="RHS"/> It has pink [[Bud|flower buds]],<ref name="RHS"/> that open up to brilliant blue or bright blue flowers with a white centre, approximately {{cvt|10|mm|1}} wide. There are 5 sepals. It has clusters of flowers, but only one flowering at a time. Its [[stamens]] are hidden inside narrow flower-tubes which end in a white eye in the centre of a blue flower.<ref name="Fitter">{{cite book |last1=Fitter |first1=Richard |last2=Fitter |first2=Alastair |title=The Wild Flowers of Britain and Europe |date=1978 |publisher=Collins |location=St James Place, London |isbn=0-00-219069-9 |edition=3}}</ref>

The flowers are pollinated by bees and bumblebees, and the seed capsules can also be transported over some distances on passing animal fur or attached to clothing.<ref name="RHS"/>

==Taxonomy==
[[File:AnchusaSempervirens-blad-hr.jpg|thumb|right|Stem and leaves of ''Pentaglottis sempervirens'']]
It is commonly known as ''evergreen-bugloss'' and ''green alkanet''.<ref name="Bennett">{{cite book |last1=Bennett |first1=Masha |title=Pulmonarias and the Borage Family |date=2003 |publisher=Timber Press |pages=175–176 |isbn=0881925896}}</ref>

The genus ''Pentaglottis'' was first published by Bohemian botanist [[Ignaz Friedrich Tausch]] (1793–1848), in Flora 12: 643 in 1829,<ref name="PowoGenus"/> then the species ''Pentaglottis sempervirens'' was first published by American botanist [[Liberty Hyde Bailey]] (1858–1954) in Man. Cult. Pl., ed. 2: 837 in 1949.<ref name="PowoSpecies">{{cite web |title=''Pentaglottis sempervirens'' (L.) Tausch ex L.H.Bailey {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:60457907-2 |website=Plants of the World Online |access-date=17 November 2023 |language=en}}</ref>

The genus name ''Pentaglottis'' is [[Greek language|Greek]], meaning "five tongues", and the species [[specific name (botany)|specific epithet]] of ''sempervirens'' is [[Latin]], and means "always alive", or "evergreen".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Coombes |first1=Allen |title=The A to Z of Plant Names: A Quick Reference Guide to 4000 Garden Plants |date=2012 |publisher=Timber Press |location=Portland, Oregon |isbn=9781604691962 |page=28}}</ref>

The word "alkanet" derives from [[Middle English]], from [[Old Spanish]] {{Lang|osp|alcaneta}}, diminutive of ''alcana'', "henna", from Medieval Latin {{Lang|la|alchanna}}, from Arabic {{Lang|ar-Latn|al-ḥinnā’}}, "[[henna]]" : ''al-'': "the" + ''ḥinnā’'', "henna". The common name of "alkanet" is also used for dyer's bugloss (''[[Alkanna tinctoria]]'') and common bugloss (''[[Anchusa officinalis]]''). 

The genus ''Pentaglottis'' has two known synonyms, ''Carylopha'' <small>Fisch. & Trautv.</small> and ''Caryolopha'' <small>Fisch. & Trautv</small>.<ref name="PowoGenus"/>

The genus and species are accepted by [[Germplasm Resources Information Network|GRIN]] ([[United States Department of Agriculture]] and the [[Agricultural Research Service]]).<ref name="Grin">{{cite web |title=Taxon: ''Pentaglottis sempervirens'' (L.) Tausch ex L.H. Bailey |url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxon/taxonomygenus?id=435073 |website=npgsweb.ars-grin.gov |access-date=17 November 2023}}</ref>

==Distribution==
[[File:Green Alkanet (Pentaglottis sempervirens) - geograph.org.uk - 801261.jpg|thumb|right|Flowers and pink flowerbud of ''Pentaglottis sempervirens'']]
The [[Native species|native]] range of this genus is south western Europe. It is [[endemic]] to France, Portugal and Spain.
It was introduced into the countries (and regions) of Australia (with the state of Tasmania) Belgium, Canada (within the province of [[British Columbia]]), Czechoslovakia, Great Britain, Ireland, Italy and the United States (within the states of California, Maine, Oregon and Washington).<ref name="PowoGenus">{{cite web |title=''Pentaglottis'' Tausch {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:4741-1 |website=Plants of the World Online |access-date=17 November 2023 |language=en}}</ref>

Green alkanet is an [[introduced species]] in the [[British Isles]].<ref>http://www.nhm.ac.uk/fff-pcp/glob.pl?report=Flora&Flora.[FloraNo]=236800{{Dead link|date=March 2026}}</ref>

==Habitat==
It is found in woods and in hedge-banks,<ref name="Fitter"/> or in damp or shaded places and often close to some buildings. It likes [[alkaline]] soils and is considered a weed in some parts of the UK.<ref name="RHS">{{cite web |title=Green alkanet / RHS Gardening |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/weeds/green-alkanet |website=www.rhs.org.uk |access-date=17 November 2023 |language=en-gb}}</ref>

==Uses==
The blue flowers of the green alkanet are edible, and are often used as a garnish for salads or drinks.

Green alkanet roots are not edible. They contain pyrrolizidine alkaloids, which are toxic to the liver, even when cooked.

Although toxic if consumed in large quantities, the leaves have medicinal properties and were recommended for the treatment of coughs, digestive problems and fevers by [[Nicholas Culpeper]].<ref>[https://myyearofstroudwildlife.blog/2020/05/23/flower-of-the-day-green-alkanet/ Stroud wildlife]</ref> The leaves were also considered an effective remedy for burns and ulcers when crushed and combined with [[vinegar]].<ref>[https://www.botanical.com/botanical/mgmh/a/alkan024.html Botanical green alkanet]</ref> In modern times the leaves and stems have been used by doctors to treat [[staphylococcus]].<ref>{{Self-published source|date=May 2024}}[https://wonderfulweedweekly.co.uk/the-boraginaceae-green-alkanet-forget-me-not-houndstongue-vipers-bugloss-oysterplant-the-gromwells-and-lungworts/ Weed weekly]</ref>
